aider:
Aider is an open-source Python-based AI pair programmer that runs entirely in the terminal. Its defining feature is git-native operation: every change the AI makes is automatically committed with a descriptive commit message, so you can use git diff, git log, and git revert to audit or undo any AI modification. This makes it uniquely safe for production codebases where tracking changes matters.

The tool processes 15 billion tokens per week across its user base as of early 2026. Aider builds a repo map — a semantic index of the entire codebase — enabling accurate multi-file edits across large projects. It connects to any LLM: Claude Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini, DeepSeek, local Ollama models, and dozens of providers via OpenRouter. The open-source community releases frequent updates.

Key capabilities include automatic git commits for every AI change, multi-file editing across large codebases via repo map, voice input mode, in-editor image support for visual debugging, and a watch mode that responds to special comments in your code. Aider works in any directory without IDE plugins or configuration beyond an API key.

Pricing: Aider is completely free and open source. You pay only for LLM API calls to your chosen provider. Running on local models via Ollama costs nothing beyond hardware.

Limitations: Aider is terminal-only — there is no GUI, IDE extension, or browser interface. Setup requires installing via pip and configuring an API key. Like all BYOK tools, LLM costs are paid separately.

Best suited for developers who live in the terminal and want an AI pair programmer with full git accountability — where every AI change is tracked, reviewable, and reversible.
bolt-new:
Bolt.new is a browser-based AI app builder that generates and deploys full-stack web applications from natural language prompts. The original Bolt gained attention in 2024 for generating frontend code quickly; Bolt V2, also called Bolt Cloud, is a substantially deeper platform with built-in infrastructure that eliminates the need to configure third-party services.

Bolt Cloud bundles everything needed for a production web app: a built-in database, authentication system, file storage, edge functions, analytics, and hosting — all managed within the Bolt platform. Users do not need to set up Supabase, Firebase, or any separate backend service. This integrated stack is the most significant architectural difference between Bolt and competitors like Lovable or Replit.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) support allows Bolt to connect external tools — Notion, Linear, Git repositories, and other MCP-compatible services — directly into the generation workflow. This makes it possible to build apps that read from a Notion database, update Linear issues on completion, or commit generated code to a Git repository automatically.

AI image generation is built into the chat interface, with WebP export for use in generated applications. Build performance has improved by 40% compared to the 2024 version, and Bolt now handles projects approximately 1,000 times larger than the original — making it viable for serious applications rather than just prototypes.

Team features include shared workspaces, team templates, admin controls, and collaborative editing, enabling multiple developers or stakeholders to work on the same Bolt project. Claude Opus 4.6 is available as a model option with adjustable reasoning intensity, allowing users to trade response speed for deeper architectural thinking on complex generation tasks.

Bolt.new is best for developers and founders who want to build and ship full-stack applications without managing separate hosting, auth, and database services, and for teams that need collaborative AI app development in a single platform.
chatgpt:
ChatGPT is OpenAI's flagship chat assistant for writing, coding, research, analysis and multimodal tasks. It works in the browser, in desktop and mobile apps, and through the API, and it has become one of the most widely used consumer AI products in the world.

As of July 2026 the default model is GPT-5.5, offered in Instant and Thinking modes, with a Pro variant on higher tiers. GPT-5.5 launched around April 2026 and replaced the older GPT-5 lineup; the model picker was simplified to Instant, Thinking and Pro. The GPT-4o era is over, and GPT-4o is no longer the flagship. A newer GPT-5.6 family (Sol flagship, Terra balanced, Luna fast) has entered limited preview but is not yet generally available.

Capabilities cover long-form and technical writing, code generation and debugging, document and image analysis, voice conversations, web browsing, data analysis, and image generation, all built on the current multimodal GPT-5.x stack rather than the older GPT-4o pipeline. Higher tiers add larger context windows and Sora video generation.

Pricing is tiered. Free is $0/mo and now shows ads to logged-in adult users in the US (since February 2026), with the default GPT-5.5 model at limited usage. The new Go tier is $8/mo and has rolled out worldwide. Plus is $20/mo. Pro is now split into two options: $100/mo with roughly 5x Plus quotas, and $200/mo with about 20x quotas plus Sora video and a 1M-token context window. Business (Team) is $25/user/mo with a two-seat minimum, and Enterprise is custom-priced.

Limitations remain real. The model can still produce confident but wrong answers, free usage is capped and now ad-supported in the US, and the most useful capabilities (long context, video, heavy quotas) sit behind the pricier tiers. GPT-5.6 is preview-only, so you cannot rely on it for production yet.

ChatGPT suits almost anyone who wants a general-purpose AI assistant, from casual users on the free or Go tier to professionals and teams who need higher quotas, larger context and collaboration features.
cursor:
Cursor is an AI-first code editor that started as a VS Code fork and has grown into a full agentic coding platform. Instead of just autocompleting lines, it can plan and carry out multi-step changes across a repository, run its own review passes, and hand work off to background agents.

The current release is Cursor 3.10, shipped June 30, 2026. The headline change is Composer 2.5, Cursor's own in-house agentic model introduced in May 2026, which the company positions as matching frontier models like Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 at roughly a tenth of the cost. Version 3.10 added team marketplaces and Team MCP servers, while 3.9 brought an iOS app (public beta) and a customization hub. The project also moved its home from cursor.sh to cursor.com.

Key capabilities include the Composer agent for large edits, cloud agents and cloud dev environments you can trigger with /in-cloud, automatic code review, and a faster, cheaper Bugbot that returns reviews in around 90 seconds. It still supports third-party models, MCP servers, custom rules, and hooks, so you are not locked into Composer.

Pricing is tiered. Hobby is free, Pro (Individual) is $20 per month, Pro+ is $60 per month, and Ultra is $200 per month; Teams costs $40 per user per month and Enterprise is custom. Billing is credit-based, with a credit pool roughly equal to the plan price, though Auto mode usage is unlimited on paid plans. Annual billing saves about 20 percent.

The main limitations are cost and complexity. Heavy agent use can burn through credits quickly, and the pricing model has changed enough over time to confuse users. Being a VS Code fork, it occasionally lags behind upstream extensions, and the most capable features assume you are comfortable letting an agent make sweeping changes.

Cursor suits developers who want an agent that can take on real multi-file tasks, not just suggest snippets. It is a strong fit for professional teams already living in VS Code, and less compelling for people who only want lightweight autocomplete or work in a non-VS-Code editor.
descript:
Descript is an editor for podcasts and video that works off a transcript: you edit the words in a document and the audio and video follow. That approach makes cutting, rearranging, and cleaning up recordings much faster than dragging clips on a traditional timeline.

The product has shifted decisively toward AI. Its headline layer is now Underlord, a generative co-editor that drafts scripts, writes show notes, automatically surfaces viral and social clips, reorganizes scenes, and can generate and extend video on its own. Classic tools like filler-word removal, noise suppression, and timing fixes are still there but are now framed as part of this AI workflow. In 2026 Descript added an AI model picker (including Claude Sonnet 4.5) so you can control reasoning and style, parallel AI media-generation jobs, automatic avoidance of letterbox and crop bars, and a public token-based API open to all users.

On the editing side you get multitrack audio and video, screen recording, layered timelines, remote recording, transcription, and AI voices, plus overdub-style corrections and translation and dubbing features.

Pricing is freemium. There is a Free plan at $0, Hobbyist at $16/user/month billed annually ($24 monthly), Creator at $24/user/month annually ($35 monthly), Business at $50/user/month annually ($65 monthly), and a custom Enterprise tier. In September 2025 the billing model was rebuilt: the old transcription-hours allowance was replaced by monthly media minutes/hours plus metered AI credits, with top-ups available.

The main limitations are cost predictability and dependence on credits. Because AI generation and media time are metered, heavy AI users can burn through their allowance and need top-ups, and the plan structure is more complex than a flat subscription. It is also a fairly heavy app that expects reasonably capable hardware.

Descript suits podcasters, video creators, marketers, and teams who want to edit by editing text and lean on AI for drafting, clipping, and cleanup rather than hand-crafting every cut on a timeline.
duolingo-max:
Duolingo Max is the premium subscription tier that sits above the free plan and the mid-level Super plan. It keeps everything Duolingo is known for — gamified lessons, streaks, and bite-sized practice — and layers AI conversation tools on top for learners who want to actually speak the language.

The AI features originally launched on GPT-4 in 2023 but are now reported to run on OpenAI's GPT-4o. The current marquee feature is Video Call: a live spoken conversation with an animated character named Lily who remembers details across sessions. It has expanded to more languages, including Japanese, Korean and Chinese. Note that in January 2026, 'Explain My Answer' stopped being a Max exclusive and became free for everyone, so Max's paid edge now rests mainly on Video Call and Roleplay.

Key capabilities include real-time spoken practice with Lily, Roleplay scenarios (ordering food, booking a hotel) where the AI plays a conversation partner, and the usual full Duolingo course library with no ads.

Pricing is tiered: the free plan is $0, Super is $95.99/year, and Duolingo Max is $167.99/year or $29.99/month. There is also a Super Family plan from $119.99/year covering up to six people, though that is Super rather than Max.

Limitations are worth weighing. Max costs almost double Super, and with 'Explain My Answer' now free, the differentiation is narrower than it once was. Video Call availability still depends on your target language, and the AI conversations, while useful, are scripted enough that they don't replace a human tutor for nuance.

Max makes sense if you're already committed to Duolingo, want spoken conversation practice, and are learning a language where Video Call is supported. Casual learners are usually fine on the free tier or Super.
github-copilot:
GitHub Copilot started as an in-editor autocomplete tool, but the current 2026 product is a full multi-model coding platform. It lives inside your editor, in the terminal and on GitHub itself, handling code completion, chat, an agent mode that edits across files, cloud agents that work on tasks asynchronously, and automated code review.

The biggest recent change came on June 1, 2026, when Copilot moved from premium request units to consumption-based GitHub AI Credits, a token-based system. Every plan now includes a monthly credit allowance, with pay-as-you-go overages and new admin budget and spending caps. The older automatic fallback to cheaper models was discontinued, and code review now also consumes GitHub Actions minutes.

The core capabilities today are agent mode, cloud agents, chat, code review, a CLI, and the ability to pick which frontier model you want, including Claude, GPT-5 and others. Code completions and Next Edit suggestions stay included and do not draw down your credit allowance.

On pricing, individuals can choose Free at 0 dollars a month (around 2,000 completions, limited chat and agent use, automatic model selection), Pro at 10 dollars a month (unlimited completions, model selection, cloud agents, a monthly credit allowance), Pro+ at 39 dollars a month (premium frontier models including Opus and a higher allowance), or Max at 100 dollars a month (the highest allowance and priority access to new models). Verified students get Pro-level access free. Organizations pick Business at 19 dollars per user a month (including 19 dollars of monthly AI Credits) or Enterprise at 39 dollars per user a month (including 39 dollars of credits, codebase indexing and GitHub.com chat). Promotional bonus credits run June through August 2026: Business plus 30 dollars a month, Enterprise plus 70 dollars a month.

The main limitation is cost predictability: usage-based billing means heavy agent, chat or frontier-model use can push you into overages, and code review burning Actions minutes adds a second meter to watch. Budgets and caps help, but teams need to monitor consumption.

Copilot is a strong fit if you already work in GitHub and VS Code, want an agentic assistant rather than plain autocomplete, and value being able to choose the underlying model. The free tier is a low-risk way to try it, while Pro+ and Max suit heavier users of premium models.
grok:
Grok is the chat assistant built by xAI, Elon Musk's AI company. It lives both inside X (formerly Twitter) and as a standalone product at grok.com, and it is known for a looser, more opinionated conversational style than most rivals, plus tight access to real-time posts on X.

The flagship model is Grok 4.3 (Beta), which became the default in April 2026. It added native video input, pushed its knowledge cutoff to December 2025, and improved tool-calling. xAI has announced Grok 4.5 for public release on July 9, 2026, pitched as an "Opus-class" model built on a new 1.5-trillion-parameter V9 foundation and trained partly on Cursor coding data.

On capabilities, Grok handles text chat, image and video understanding, web and X search, and image/video generation through Grok Imagine. Developers can also reach the models through the xAI API.

Pricing spans a wide ladder. The free tier is $0 and now runs a lighter Grok 4 Mini, text only, capped at roughly 10 prompts every 2 hours. Paid options include X Premium at $8/mo, SuperGrok Lite at $10/mo, SuperGrok at $30/mo (or $300/yr, about 17% off), X Premium+ at $40/mo, and SuperGrok Heavy at $300/mo. The API (grok-4.3) costs $1.25 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens.

The main limitation is the free tier, which was tightened in March 2026: image and video generation were removed from it and it only runs Grok 4 Mini with a tight prompt cap. Getting the full flagship experience and Grok Imagine requires a paid plan.

Grok suits people already active on X who want an assistant wired into live posts, users who like a more candid tone, and developers who want a competitively priced API. Anyone who needs the newest model or heavy image/video generation should expect to pay.
julius-ai:
Julius AI is a data analysis platform where you talk to your data in plain language. You point it at a dataset or a database, ask questions, and it writes and runs the underlying code, returns charts and tables, and explains the results. It started as a CSV-and-charts chatbot, but it has grown well beyond that.

There is no traditional product version number anymore. Julius now describes itself as an 'AI-powered Data Agents' platform that runs current frontier models. The July 2026 pricing page lists access to GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, with a comparison table also referencing Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7, plus an 'All Julius Models' option. The biggest recent change is billing: it moved from the old message-count quota (the '15 messages a month' free tier many 2025 write-ups mention) to a credit-based system.

Capability-wise it now handles far more than a single CSV. You get live database connectors for Postgres, BigQuery and Snowflake, export to slides, HTML and charts, custom agents, a Julius Slack agent, semantic schema learning so it understands your table structures, and scheduled runs for recurring reports.

Pricing is freemium with two billing modes. On yearly billing (default, marketed as 20% off and shown per month): Free $0; Plus $16/mo (24,000 credits/yr); Pro $37/mo (60,000 credits/yr, 32 GB RAM); Max $166/mo (300,000 credits/yr); Ultra $416/mo (840,000 credits/yr); Business $375/mo (720,000 credits/yr, up to 50 members, database connectors). Monthly billing runs higher: Plus $20/mo, Pro $45/mo, Business $450/mo, with Enterprise as custom Contact Us pricing. The free tier includes about 2,000 credits per month, 2 GB RAM, a Google Drive connector and needs no card; students and educators are reportedly offered 50% off via third-party sources.

The main limitation is the credit model itself: heavy or complex jobs burn credits quickly, and the free 2,000 credits and 2 GB RAM run out fast on real workloads. Database connectors are gated to Business and up, and results still need a human check because the agent can make analytical mistakes.

Julius suits analysts, founders, researchers and operations people who want to query data conversationally without writing SQL or Python, and who occasionally need to connect a real database or ship a report. If you only ever open a single spreadsheet once in a while, the free tier is enough; if you live in databases, budget for Business.
microsoft-copilot:
Microsoft Copilot is the AI assistant Microsoft has woven across Windows, Edge, Bing, and the Microsoft 365 apps. It handles conversational chat, web search with cited answers, image generation, document drafting, and in the paid tiers it works directly inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook.

The biggest recent change is the model. Copilot has moved off GPT-4 onto the GPT-5 family. GPT-5 became the consumer default in the October-November 2025 rollout, GPT-5.4 Thinking reached Microsoft 365 Copilot in March 2026, and GPT-5.5 is rolling out now. Copilot Chat added GPT-5.2 with an Auto/Instant/Thinking selector, and Anthropic's Claude models (Sonnet 4.5/4.6 and Opus) are now selectable inside Copilot too.

Day to day you get Smart mode and Think Deeper for harder questions, voice conversations, web search that returns answers with citations, and roughly 15 image-generation boosts per day on the free tier. July 2026 also added AI-content watermarking and a rebuilt Copilot Notebooks experience that reached general availability.

Pricing splits into consumer and business. Copilot Free costs nothing and covers chat with the latest GPT models when capacity allows, cited web search, Think Deeper, voice, and the daily image boosts. Microsoft 365 Personal (about $9.99/mo) and Family (about $12.99/mo) raise Copilot usage limits. Microsoft 365 Premium at $19.99/mo replaced the retired standalone Copilot Pro and adds the highest consumer limits, Copilot inside the Office apps, Designer, and up to 6 TB of storage.

For organizations, the Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on is $18.00/user/mo on an annual promo (down from $21) or $25.20 monthly; Business Standard with Copilot runs $23.50 yearly, Business Premium with Copilot $32.00 yearly, and the enterprise add-on lands around $30/user/mo. Copilot Studio for building custom agents is $200/mo. Note the standalone Copilot Pro was sunset in late 2025 and existing subscriptions only work until August 1, 2026.

The main limitations: the free tier throttles priority model access to when capacity allows and caps image generation, the strongest features are tied to a Microsoft 365 subscription, and the tiering across consumer, business, and enterprise SKUs is genuinely confusing. Copilot makes the most sense if you already live in Microsoft 365 and want an assistant that reaches into your documents, mail, and calendar rather than a standalone chatbot.
microsoft-copilot-studio:
Microsoft Copilot Studio is Microsoft's low-code environment for designing, testing and publishing AI agents. It sits inside the Power Platform and Microsoft 365 ecosystem, letting makers wire agents to enterprise data, Teams, Dynamics 365 and third-party APIs without heavy custom code.

The current version is 2026 release wave 1, running on platform build 2026.6.2 (June 2026). This wave brought several substantial changes: computer-using agents reached general availability, and a new orchestration layer improves accuracy on evaluations by roughly 20% while cutting token consumption by about 50%. Real-time speech-to-speech voice agents were added for Dynamics 365 Contact Center, and multi-step workflows were redesigned so UI-driven agents run alongside API actions and approvals.

On the capability side, the platform now supports multi-agent orchestration, autonomous computer-using agents and a broader model choice. In the Prompt Tool you can select GPT-5.5 Reasoning (early release) or Anthropic Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.5, offered as a paid experimental preview in the US.

Pricing runs entirely on Copilot Credits, which replaced the old per-message billing on September 1, 2025 (same quantity and rate). A prepaid capacity pack is $200 per pack per month for 25,000 Copilot Credits; pay-as-you-go is metered at $0.01 per credit with no upfront commitment but requires an Azure subscription. A one-year Copilot Credit Commit Units (CCCU) prepurchase can save up to 20%. Building agents is included at no extra cost with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license at $30 per user per month, billed annually.

The main limitation is that there is no free production tier. The free authoring or maker license costs $0 but only works if the tenant already holds a paid prepaid Copilot Credit pack, and the individual free trial license is time-limited and cannot publish agents. In practice, deploying anything requires payment.

Copilot Studio suits organizations already invested in Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 or Azure that want governed, low-code agents connected to their existing data. It is a weaker fit for individuals or small teams wanting a genuinely free way to ship an agent to production.
n8n:
n8n is a workflow automation tool that lets you wire together apps, databases and APIs through a visual editor, with the option to drop into code when you need it. It runs self-hosted or in the cloud.

The product has moved to the 2.x release line, with n8n@2.29.8 as the current stable build (released July 8, 2026) and 2.30.x in pre-release. The big 2026 change is that AI and agents are now front and center: the AI Agent node was rebuilt with structured tool calling for Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, Mistral, Groq and OpenAI-compatible models, four memory backends (in-memory, Redis, Postgres, Motorhead) and a ReAct execution mode. The flat builder was replaced by a spatial Canvas UI introduced in v1.30.

Beyond AI, recent versions add per-node retry with exponential backoff, 35+ new native integrations (including dedicated Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Groq, Perplexity and ElevenLabs nodes for a total of 500+), expanded admin controls, public API access and more enterprise auth options. Cloud plans now bundle monthly AI credits: 2,300 on Starter, up to 13,700 on Pro.

Pricing is genuinely tiered. The self-hosted Community Edition is free ($0) with unlimited executions and every integration, plus a 14-day cloud trial. Paid cloud tiers run Starter at EUR 24/mo, Pro at EUR 60/mo, Business at EUR 800/mo and custom Enterprise; annual billing is roughly 17% cheaper (about EUR 20, 50 and 667 respectively). A start-up program offers 50% off Business for companies under 20 employees.

The main limitations are honest ones: n8n is fair-code under the Sustainable Use License, not OSI-approved open source, so commercial resale is restricted. Self-hosting means you own the maintenance, and the paid cloud pricing steps up sharply between Pro and Business.

It suits developers and technical teams who want automation they can host and audit themselves, and who increasingly want to build AI-agent workflows without stitching together separate tools.
nano-banana:
Nano Banana is an AI-powered image generation and editing platform built on Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash Image model — and its Pro version runs on Gemini 3 Pro Image. Unlike text-to-image tools that generate from scratch, Nano Banana specializes in in-context editing: you upload a photo, describe the changes in plain language, and the model applies them while preserving the original composition, lighting and scene structure.

The standout feature is character consistency. Most AI image tools struggle to keep the same face, outfit or object looking identical across multiple edits or scenes. Nano Banana was built specifically to solve this — making it the go-to tool for serialized content creators, AI influencers, branded campaigns and game asset pipelines where visual coherence across images is non-negotiable.

The free tier offers credits on sign-up with no install required — everything runs in the browser. Nano Banana Pro unlocks 4K resolution, advanced multi-step editing, sharp text rendering and higher-volume generation. For designers, marketers and content creators who need precise, repeatable AI image editing — Nano Banana delivers results competing tools consistently struggle to match.
perplexity:
Perplexity is a conversational search tool that answers questions with cited, up-to-date sources instead of a list of links. It sits somewhere between a chatbot and a search engine, and over 2026 it has leaned hard into research and agentic work.

The headline change is Advanced Deep Research. It is no longer a simple multi-page report mode: it now runs agentically inside Perplexity Computer, asks clarifying questions before it starts, accepts follow-ups mid-run, and shows live source and progress tracking. On Pro and Max, Deep Research is powered by Claude Opus 4.5/4.6, and Perplexity reports state-of-the-art benchmark scores (93.9% on SimpleQA, 21.1% on Humanity's Last Exam). The Deep Research in Computer agentic assistant shipped on June 19, 2026, adding a command panel, thread forking, inline actions, analytics APIs, and enterprise credit controls.

Beyond research, Perplexity gives you multi-model access to GPT-5, Claude, Gemini and o3-pro, a Model Council feature that compares several models side by side, and the Comet browser for AI-assisted browsing.

Pricing runs across five tiers. Free is $0 and includes roughly 5 Pro searches per day. Pro is $20/mo or $200/yr, bundles $5/mo of Sonar API credits, and allows about 20 Deep Research runs a day. The new Max tier is $200/mo or $2,000/yr and adds Model Council, 10,000 Computer credits a month, Sora 2 Pro video and Nano Banana Pro image generation, and unlimited Labs. Students get Pro for around $10/mo, and there are Enterprise Pro (~$40/seat/mo) and Enterprise Max (~$325/seat/mo) plans.

The limitations are worth knowing. Like any AI system it can still misread or over-trust weak sources, so citations need checking. The most capable features sit behind the $200/mo Max tier and a monthly Computer credit budget, the free tier is quite tight, and juggling multiple models plus Model Council adds a learning curve.

Perplexity is a strong pick if you do a lot of source-backed research, want agentic Deep Research on top-tier models, or like comparing several AI models on the same question. Casual users who just need a few answers a day can stay on Free, while heavy or enterprise users will find the paid tiers built around them.
uxpilot:
UX Pilot is an AI-assisted product design tool aimed at UX/UI designers who want to move from idea to high-fidelity screens quickly. Instead of starting from a blank canvas, you describe what you need and the tool generates full interfaces you can refine.

There is no public model version number. Instead, UX Pilot offers three generation modes: Standard, Deep Design, and Max, which trade higher credit cost for more elaborate output. Through 2026 the product added the Nodey plugin for generating and editing components directly inside Figma, AI UX-research with attention-prediction, and design-to-code that converts an image into HTML. It now runs direct comparison pages against Anthropic's Claude Design (Claude Opus 4.7) and other AI design tools.

Key capabilities include text-to-UI generation, in-Figma editing via Nodey, attention heatmaps and UX-research feedback, and image-to-HTML export for handing work to developers.

Pricing is credit-based. The Free plan is $0 with 45 credits (recent reviews describe these as one-time, not monthly) covering up to about 7 screens. Standard is $14/month billed annually ($19 monthly) with 420 credits, roughly 70 screens. Pro is $22/month billed annually ($29 monthly) with 1,200 credits, around 200 screens, marked Popular. Teams is $31/user/month billed annually ($39 monthly) with 1,600 credits per user, about 266 screens. Enterprise is custom, with unlimited or custom credits and model fine-tuning.

The main limitation is the credit economy: credits do not roll over, and the richer Deep Design and Max modes burn roughly 12 to 18 credits per screen versus about 6 in Standard, so heavy or high-detail use consumes budget fast. The free tier's credits are one-time rather than a recurring allowance.

It suits designers and small teams who want fast AI-generated screens, Figma users who want generation inside their existing workflow, and anyone who needs quick design-to-HTML output. Teams with steady high-volume needs should model the credit burn before committing.
whisper:
Whisper is a family of open-source speech recognition models released by OpenAI. It transcribes spoken audio into text and can translate speech from many languages directly into English. The weights are published under the permissive MIT license, so you can download them and run them on your own hardware.

The current open release is large-v3-turbo, a distilled model introduced in October 2024. It keeps almost all of the accuracy of the full large-v3 model while running about 8x faster, which makes it far more practical for batch jobs and near-real-time use. The full large-v3 checkpoint is still available when you want the highest possible quality.

Alongside the open models, OpenAI now offers hosted transcription through its API. The classic endpoint is whisper-1, and it has since been joined by GPT-4o-based models: gpt-4o-transcribe and the cheaper gpt-4o-mini-transcribe, which add options like speaker diarization. According to reports, a streaming variant, gpt-realtime-whisper, arrived around May 2026 and returns transcript deltas live as you speak.

Pricing splits into two tracks. The open-source models are free: you pay only for your own compute. The hosted API is usage-based: whisper-1 and gpt-4o-transcribe are $0.006 per minute ($0.36/hr), gpt-4o-mini-transcribe is $0.003 per minute ($0.18/hr), and the live gpt-realtime-whisper runs about $0.017 per minute.

Accuracy varies a lot by language. Whisper was trained on around 99 languages, but the quality is strongest for high-resource languages like English and drops noticeably for less common ones. Running the larger models locally also needs a capable GPU, and the model can occasionally hallucinate text during long silences.

Whisper is a good fit if you want a free, self-hostable transcription engine, need broad multilingual coverage, or want a managed API without building your own pipeline. Choose the hosted GPT-4o models if you need diarization or live streaming out of the box.
writesonic:
Writesonic started life as an AI copywriting tool, but the current product is positioned as an AI Search Visibility Platform focused on generative engine optimization (GEO). The core job now is tracking where and how your brand shows up inside AI answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews.

The latest version brings AI Article Writer 6.0, which uses a recursive research-outline-write loop rather than a single prompt-to-text pass. Under the hood the platform was rebuilt on a new in-house Writesonic model alongside integrated GPT-5 and Claude 4.5, and the company says more than 20 features were refreshed in this cycle.

Key capabilities include the GEO tracking dashboard, an Action Center that flags missing prompts and citation opportunities and tells you what to do about them, dedicated AI agents for SEO, content and LinkedIn, and sentiment analysis of how your brand is described in AI responses.

On pricing, the official site lists Starter around $79/mo, Basic around $199/mo, Growth around $399/mo (marked most popular) and a custom Enterprise tier, with roughly 20% off on annual billing. There is a free trial with full access and no card required, plus a limited free tier for basic SEO and content tools.

Be aware that pricing is genuinely confusing: the site is ambiguous about monthly versus annual rates, and at least one third-party source lists a different ladder (Lite $49, Standard $99, Professional $249, Advanced $499), which suggests real monthly rates may be higher than the headline numbers imply. The entry point is also far above Writesonic's old cheap plans.

This platform suits SEO teams, agencies and marketers who care about brand visibility inside AI search and want writing plus tracking in one place. If you just need occasional cheap AI copy, the current pricing and GEO focus will feel like overkill.
zed:
Zed is a code editor built entirely in Rust, designed from the ground up for performance and low latency. Version 1.0, released April 29, 2026, marks a five-year development milestone and the first stable release suitable for production teams. The editor is fast by design — Rust eliminates the overhead that slows Electron-based editors like VS Code and Cursor under heavy load.

The flagship feature of Zed 1.0 is Parallel Agents: users can run multiple AI agents simultaneously, each working on a different part of the codebase independently. One agent can refactor a module while another writes tests for a second module and a third agent handles documentation — all concurrently. This is a meaningful productivity gain over single-threaded agent workflows that require waiting for one task to finish before starting the next.

In January 2026, Zed co-authored the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) with JetBrains, establishing a cross-editor standard for how AI agents communicate with development environments. ACP means agents built for Zed can also run in JetBrains IDEs and vice versa, reducing vendor lock-in in the AI coding agent ecosystem.

Model support in Zed 1.0 includes GPT-5.5, DeepSeek V4, and MiMo V2.5, giving developers access to a range of frontier models directly inside the editor without configuring separate API keys per provider. Git graph view and split diffs are new interface features that improve code review workflows within the editor itself.

Zed is free for individual developers. The Business plan adds organization-wide AI policy enforcement, centralized billing, and AI governance controls — useful for engineering teams that need to manage model access and usage across large groups.

Zed is best for developers who want a fast, resource-efficient editor with serious parallel AI agent capability, and for teams that need centralized AI governance without adopting a heavyweight enterprise tool.
